nameStory: The 'scintillans' in this nudibranch's scientific name means 'sparkling' or 'glittering' in Latin, referring to the tiny reflective spots that dot its translucent body. When light hits these microscopic structures just right underwater, the little sea slug seems to twinkle like a living jewel. It's nature's own underwater disco ball, though you'll need sharp eyes and good lighting to catch the sparkle!
description: The sparkling nudibranch is a tiny sea slug that looks like a translucent caterpillar decorated with colorful finger-like projections. These marine creatures are shell-less mollusks that crawl along underwater surfaces using their muscular foot. Most individuals are less than half an inch long, making them one of the smaller nudibranchs you might encounter. Their bodies are typically clear to whitish with orange, red, or pink highlights, especially on the tips of their numerous spiky projections called cerata.

idTips.label: Body projections (cerata)
idTips.description: Numerous finger-like projections extending from the back and sides, each tipped with bright orange or red coloring that looks like tiny flames

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Very small, typically 8-15mm long (about the size of your pinky nail), requiring close examination to see details

idTips.label: Body texture
idTips.description: Translucent, jelly-like body that feels soft and squishy to gentle touch, with a slightly sticky surface

idTips.label: Head tentacles
idTips.description: Two pairs of tentacles on the head - the upper rhinophores are club-shaped and slightly wrinkled, while the oral tentacles are smoother

idTips.label: Movement
idTips.description: Glides smoothly along surfaces with a wave-like motion of its foot, leaving no visible slime trail

idTips.label: Sparkling effect
idTips.description: Tiny reflective spots throughout the body create subtle glittering when viewed under bright light or flashlight beam

habitat: Found in shallow coastal waters of New England, typically 6-60 feet deep on rocky substrates, pier pilings, and kelp forests. Look for them crawling on hydroids (their preferred food), especially on the undersides of rocks and in crevices where the water stays calm. They prefer areas with good water circulation but protection from strong currents.

seasonality.spring: Most active as waters warm, often found in shallow tide pools and on dock pilings where hydroid colonies are beginning their spring growth.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period with highest numbers visible. Best time for spotting them during low tides on warm, calm days.
seasonality.fall: Still active but becoming less common as they move to deeper waters. Look for them on protected sides of rocks and structures.
seasonality.winter: Rarely seen in shallow waters as they retreat to deeper, more stable temperature zones below typical diving depths.

funFact: This tiny nudibranch can steal the stinging cells from the hydroids it eats and store them in the tips of its finger-like projections, essentially turning itself into a living pincushion that can sting predators with borrowed weapons!
confusionNotes: Often confused with other small nudibranchs, but the bright orange or red-tipped cerata arranged in clusters are distinctive. Remember: 'Sparkling tips mean sparkling nudibranch' - the colorful cerata tips are your best clue, unlike other species that have more uniform coloring.
contextualKnowledge: The term 'nudibranch' literally means 'naked gill' because these sea slugs breathe through exposed, decorative projections instead of hidden gills like most mollusks. Despite their delicate appearance, nudibranchs are actually highly specialized predators with some of the most sophisticated chemical defenses in the ocean.
compareHints: The sparkling nudibranch differs from its relatives by having distinctly club-shaped rhinophores and cerata arranged in tight clusters rather than rows. The club-gilled nudibranch (Eubranchus pallidus) is larger and paler with less colorful cerata tips, while the minute aeolis (Eubranchus exiguus) is even smaller and lacks the distinctive orange-red cerata tips that make the sparkling nudibranch so recognizable.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to its relatives like the minute aeolis, the club-gilled nudibranch has more distinctly club-shaped cerata rather than pointed ones.
The Minute Aeolis is much smaller than its relative the club-gilled nudibranch (Eubranchus pallidus), which grows larger and has more club-shaped rather than finger-like cerata.
